newsitem.title: USA: Two Simpson trials a tale of stark contrast.
newsitem.headline: Two Simpson trials a tale of stark contrast.

text.p: O.J. Simpson's criminal and civil trials reached their shockingly different conclusions because the civil case heard fresh evidence and personal testimony from the former football star, legal experts said Wednesday.

In the criminal trial, in which Simpson was acquitted of murdering his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman, the jurors did not have the photographs of Simpson wearing Bruno Magli shoes and they did not hear from the defendant on the witness stand.

The photos of Simpson wearing the style of shoes that left a bloody sole-print at the murder scene were seen as pivotal in the civil trial jury's verdict on Tuesday that Simpson was responsible for the June 12, 1994, murders.

The criminal trial jurors, who reached their verdict in October 1995, also did not hear that Simpson failed a lie detector test and they did not have Nicole Brown Simpson's diaries and her undated letter accusing her then-husband of beating "the holy hell" out of her.

Nor did they hear from a counsellor at a battered women's shelter who said she received a call from someone identifying herself as "Nicole" a few days before the murders who complained that her ex-husband was "stalking" her.

All this evidence was available to the jury in the civil trial, which, in addition to finding Simpson responsible for the murders, ordered him to pay compensatory damages of $8.5 million. The punitive damages phase of the trial was set to begin on Thursday.

Significantly, the analysts said, the civil trial jurors were not allowed to hear from former detective Mark Fuhrman, who told the criminal trial he discovered a bloody glove at Simpson's estate on the day after the murders that matched one found at the crime scene.

Fuhrman was discredited during the criminal trial when Simpson's defence showed him to be a liar in denying that he had used the racial slur "nigger" in the previous 10 years. He subsequently pleaded no contest to a charge of perjury and was fined and placed on probation.

Peter Arenella, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, said the most important factors in the civil case were the shoe photographs and Simpson's grilling on the witness stand by the plaintiffs' lead attorney, Daniel Petrocelli.

Pointing out that Simpson's defence team conceded the murderer wore Bruno Magli shoes, Arenella said, "You don't have to be a rocket scientist to understand the incriminating significance of those photos.

"To believe in a conspiracy concerning such photos and their fabrication you would have to conclude that a psychic was involved in the conspiracy since one of those photos was published long before the murders occurred."
Simpson had denied ever owning the expensive Italian-made designer shoes, calling them "ugly-ass," and his defence argued that the photos were faked.

Calling Simpson "the poster child for the privilege against self-incrimination," Arenella said the defendant was able, under the law, to exercise that privilege in the criminal trial, but not in the civil trial.
"And this (civil trial) jury clearly saw there was the world according to O.J. Simpson and the world according to everyone else," Arenella said.

Harland Braun, a prominent Los Angeles criminal lawyer, agreed. "The plaintiffs in the civil case were able to successfully question Simpson's credibility, and the photos of the shoes crystalized everything, they proved him to be a liar," he said.
Braun added that the plaintiffs' lawyers also had the benefit of hindsight and did not repeat the glaring errors made by the prosecution in the criminal trial.
Arenella said Simpson's defence team would certainly appeal the verdict but they were not likely to succeed.

"Judge (Hiroshi) Fujisaki seemed from the very beginning of this (civil) case bent on helping the plaintiffs as much as possible ... But I don't believe the appeal will be successful because the California appellate courts can simply say any error committed by Fujisaki was harmless because of the independent, overwhelming evidence implicating Simpson in the murders."
